doc.title: Bob Hardaway interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: How live variety shows were produced, and their decline
summary: Shows were done in two days with pre-recorded music and two taped performances, so the band sat watching. The shows shared one format, over-exposed guests, and no musical variety shows exist now.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Well I’ll tell you the way — almost all live television shows were done the same. They were done in two days. You had a rehearsal and a pre-record the night before, which you would pre-record most of the important music. And then when the show was live, like they usually, during this one period of time there was almost always a chorus of maybe six singers, plus a dance group. And they had musical numbers that were quite extravagant. And so those were sort of tricky, and so the band didn’t have to play over and over and over again, they would pre-record them. Sometimes they’d have to be re- done. And they would tape the show twice. What they called a dress rehearsal and then the so-called main show. Both of them had audiences. And then they would pick the best of the two. But most of the music was pre-recorded. Mostly we’d just play a little [scats] a play out or something, just a couple bar incidental music. Occasionally there’d be a live number and we’d do the whole thing, but most of it was prerecorded. So a lot of this time © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
when all this wonderful stuff was going on, the comedy, we weren’t actually playing, so we could just sit there and enjoy it.
You could be in the audience too.
It must have kept quite a number of arrangers pretty busy too.

Yes it did. Yeah that was a very busy period, the 60s and 70s of live television. Unfortunately the shows, almost all of them had pretty much the same format. There’d be the principal, like Dean or Carol Burnett or whoever. And then they’d have guests, and the principal would do their shtick, and then they’d do bits with the guest, and then there would be the musical numbers and whatever. So whenever somebody would come to town, they would book them on four or five of these shows, somebody that didn’t live here.

And they were in town maybe for a week, and they’d book them, and so they just overexposed a lot of things I think. And so now there aren’t any musical variety shows now. I mean you can’t call the talk shows musical variety shows, because they really aren’t. Once in a while they’ll have a musical number, but it’s far from the kind of background music that they had in those early shows.
